Lessons.Title: Filling Containers
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: describe how water volume and surface height are related as different shapes of containers are filled, attending to cross-sectional area.

A straight-sided container with constant horizontal cross-section has volume proportional to water height. For a container that widens upward, each additional centimeter of height needs more water than the preceding centimeter.

Original comparison: pour equal 100-mL portions into a tall narrow rectangular container and a wider one. Record water heights and discuss where a linear graph is justified. Teacher-scored diagrams and observations matter; predictions cannot replace actual measurements.

Original first-party Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, 2017–2019 (CC BY 4.0), source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/11/preparation.html . No publisher figures or branded assessment tasks are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cross-sectional area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Area of a horizontal slice of the container.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 20 cm² base fills at 5 cm height with 100 cm³.

KeyConcepts.Title: Constant-fill area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal volume increments raise water by equal heights.
KeyConcepts.Example: Adding 40 cm³ to base 20 cm² raises water 2 cm.

KeyConcepts.Title: Variable area
KeyConcepts.Definition: Area changes as height changes.
KeyConcepts.Example: A widening vessel rises more slowly at high fill levels.

WorkedExamples.Title: Prism fill height
WorkedExamples.Question: Rectangular container base 20 cm² holds 100 cm³. Find water height.

WorkedExamples.Title: Extra water
WorkedExamples.Question: Same container receives 40 cm³ extra. Height rise?

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare widths
WorkedExamples.Question: Two rectangular vessels have base areas 20 and 40 cm². Pour 80 cm³ into each. Which water height is larger?
WorkedExamples.Answer: 4 cm versus 2 cm; narrow vessel is higher.
WorkedExamples.Check: The equal volumes occupy different heights.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming all containers fill at constant height rate.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Changing cross-sectional area changes height response.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing volume with height units.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: cm³ and cm are different dimensions.

SummaryPoints: Fill rate depends on cross-sectional area.
Uniform prisms give linear volume-height relations.
Varying shapes may yield nonlinear graphs.

Visuals.Title: Volume and height in a right prism
Visuals.Description: Height is volume divided by constant base area 20 cm².

Lessons.Title: How Much Will Fit?
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: estimate and compare capacities of solids using cubic units and known prism geometry, explaining which measurement determines how much fits.

Count unit cubes in a rectangular prism as layers: base area times number of layers. If physical dimensions are measured in centimeters, capacity is in cubic centimeters; 1 cubic centimeter equals 1 milliliter.

Construct two small paper containers with the same height but different bases. Predict capacities first and then verify with unit cubes or water where safe. Teacher review assesses the physical representation.

Original first-party Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, 2017–2019 (CC BY 4.0), source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/12/preparation.html . No publisher figures or branded assessment tasks are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit cube
KeyConcepts.Definition: A cube with edge length one unit.

KeyConcepts.Title: Prism capacity
KeyConcepts.Definition: Volume from base area and height.

KeyConcepts.Title: Capacity units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Cubic centimeters relate to milliliters.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rectangular volume
WorkedExamples.Question: Find volume of a 2 by 3 by 4 cm prism.
WorkedExamples.Check: Count as four layers of six cubes.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare containers
WorkedExamples.Question: One prism is 2×3×4 cm; another is 3×3×4 cm. Which holds more?

WorkedExamples.Title: Convert capacity
WorkedExamples.Question: A prism occupies 250 cm³. How many milliliters?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding dimensions rather than multiplying them.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Volume counts 3D unit cubes.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting square units for volume.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Capacity is three-dimensional.

SummaryPoints: Prism layers multiply base area by height.
Convert cm³ to mL when appropriate.

Lessons.Title: The Volume of a Cylinder
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: develop and apply V=πr²h for a right circular cylinder using circular base area and height.
A cylinder is a stack of congruent circles. The circular base has area πr², so multiplying that area by vertical height gives volume. Radius is half diameter; never substitute diameter directly as r.

Construct an original paper cylinder with marked radius and height and discuss the relationship between a circle drawing and a 3D solid. A teacher checks labeling and reasoning; numeric formula substitution is a separate graded task.

Original first-party Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, 2017–2019 (CC BY 4.0), source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/13/preparation.html . No publisher figures or branded assessment tasks are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cylinder base
KeyConcepts.Definition: A circular disk with radius r.
KeyConcepts.Example: Radius 3 cm gives base area 9π cm².

KeyConcepts.Title: Cylinder volume
KeyConcepts.Definition: Base area times perpendicular height.

KeyConcepts.Title: Radius versus diameter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Radius is half of a diameter.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute exact cylinder
WorkedExamples.Question: Radius 3 cm, height 5 cm. Find exact volume.

WorkedExamples.Title: Diameter input
WorkedExamples.Question: Diameter 8 cm, height 2 cm. What is volume?
WorkedExamples.Check: The diameter must not be squared as the radius.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare heights
WorkedExamples.Question: Two cylinders have same r and heights 3 and 9. Volume ratio?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using d² instead of r².
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Diameter is twice radius and produces fourfold volume error.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting πrh rather than πr²h.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Base area is quadratic in radius.

Visuals.Title: Cylinder volume and height
Visuals.Description: For fixed radius 3, V=9πh, so the table shows the exact coefficient V/π.

Lessons.Title: Finding Cylinder Dimensions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: use a known cylinder volume to solve for an unknown height or radius, distinguishing exact algebraic values from rounded physical measurements.
Rearrange V=πr²h. For known radius, h=V/(πr²). For known height, r=√(V/(πh)), taking the nonnegative root because physical radius cannot be negative.

Use a first-party container-design task in which a required capacity and fixed radius determine height. Explain how a change in diameter affects required height. Teacher-scored diagrams complement numerical algebra.

Original first-party Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, 2017–2019 (CC BY 4.0), source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/14/preparation.html . No publisher figures or branded assessment tasks are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Solve for height
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rearrange cylinder volume with known r.

KeyConcepts.Title: Solve for radius
KeyConcepts.Definition: Isolate squared radius first.

KeyConcepts.Title: Physical dimensions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Radius and height are nonnegative lengths.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find height
WorkedExamples.Question: Cylinder volume 72π cm³ and radius 3 cm. Find h.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find radius
WorkedExamples.Question: Volume 50π cm³ and height 2 cm. Find radius.

WorkedExamples.Title: Change radius at fixed volume
WorkedExamples.Question: A cylinder radius doubles and volume stays fixed. How must height change?
Steps: Doubling r multiplies base area by 4.
To preserve total volume, multiply height by 1/4.
New height is one quarter of original.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Taking a negative square root as physical radius.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Length cannot be negative.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignoring radius squared when solving.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Area scales quadratically with r.

SummaryPoints: Radii come from nonnegative square roots.

Lessons.Title: The Volume of a Cone
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: connect a cone with a cylinder of equal base radius and perpendicular height to justify V=(1/3)πr²h.
Three ideal equal-base equal-height cones fill the volume of the matching cylinder. The slant height is not the perpendicular height needed for the volume formula.

Draw a cone and its circumscribing cylinder, mark the same vertical height, and compare capacity through an original measure-and-pour investigation. Teacher assessment checks visual reasoning; formula calculations alone do not prove construction parity.

Original first-party Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, 2017–2019 (CC BY 4.0), source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/15/preparation.html . No publisher figures or branded assessment tasks are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cone volume
KeyConcepts.Definition: One-third of same-base, same-height cylinder.

KeyConcepts.Title: Perpendicular height
KeyConcepts.Definition: Distance straight from apex to base plane.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use this h, not side slant.
KeyConcepts.Example: A slant of 5 and radius 3 gives height 4.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cylinder comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Same r,h cylinder is three times the cone volume.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute cone
WorkedExamples.Question: Cone radius 3 cm and height 6 cm. Find volume.

WorkedExamples.Title: Slant to height
WorkedExamples.Question: Right cone radius 3 cm and slant height 5 cm. Find perpendicular h.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare equal cylinders
WorkedExamples.Question: Cylinder and cone same base and height; cylinder 60 cm³. Cone volume?
Steps: Cone is one-third of matching cylinder.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using slant height in volume formula.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Formula requires perpendicular height.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forgetting one third.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Cone fills one-third the matching cylinder.

SummaryPoints: Same-base cylinder comparison provides the factor.

Lessons.Title: Finding Cone Dimensions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: solve the cone-volume equation for an unknown height or radius given other dimensions, with exact expressions and physical constraints.
From V=πr²h/3, solve h=3V/(πr²). For known height solve r=√(3V/(πh)), selecting the nonnegative root. Respect cubic versus linear units.
Design a cone-shaped container of a specified capacity and one fixed dimension. A teacher reviews dimensional interpretation and geometry while exact number checks verify algebra.

Original first-party Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, 2017–2019 (CC BY 4.0), source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/16/preparation.html . No publisher figures or branded assessment tasks are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cone height inverse
KeyConcepts.Definition: Solve for h.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cone radius inverse
KeyConcepts.Definition: Solve for r.

KeyConcepts.Title: Physical domain
KeyConcepts.Definition: Valid solid dimensions are nonnegative.
KeyConcepts.Example: Use positive square root for r.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find cone height
WorkedExamples.Question: V=24π cm³ and r=2 cm. Find h.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find cone radius
WorkedExamples.Question: V=12π cm³, h=9 cm. Find r.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare dimensions
WorkedExamples.Question: If cone r is doubled and height unchanged, what happens to volume?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Leaving the factor of three on the wrong side.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Cone inverse differs from cylinder inverse.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply volume by 3 before dividing base area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Taking negative physical radius.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Geometry uses a nonnegative length.

Lessons.Title: Scaling One Dimension
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: predict volume change when one dimension of a prism, cylinder or similar cross-section solid changes while others remain fixed.

When only height doubles, volume doubles for a fixed base. If only a rectangular length doubles, volume doubles. When only radius of a cylinder doubles, volume quadruples because it changes two base-area directions.

Use original rectangular-box models with colored unit-cube layers to distinguish scaling one linear height from scaling a circular radius. A teacher reviews the diagram and explanation of unchanged dimensions.

Original first-party Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, 2017–2019 (CC BY 4.0), source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/17/preparation.html . No publisher figures or branded assessment tasks are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: One linear dimension
KeyConcepts.Definition: A prism dimension multiplied by k while others fixed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cylinder height
KeyConcepts.Definition: Only h changes.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cylinder radius
KeyConcepts.Definition: Only r changes but two-dimensional base area changes.

WorkedExamples.Title: Double box height
WorkedExamples.Question: Box 2×3×4 doubles height from 4 to 8. New volume?
WorkedExamples.Method: Multiply unchanged base by new h.

WorkedExamples.Title: Triple cylinder height
WorkedExamples.Question: Cylinder volume 20π grows to three times height, same radius. New volume?

WorkedExamples.Title: Double cylinder radius
WorkedExamples.Question: Cylinder originally 20π, same height but radius doubles. New volume?
Steps: New radius squared is 4 times original.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming radius acts as one independent dimension in πr².
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Radius changes two area dimensions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Changing an unmentioned dimension.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The task asks only one dimension to change.

SummaryPoints: Volume response depends on which dimension changes.

Lessons.Title: Scaling Two Dimensions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: reason about volume when two dimensions vary independently, multiplying their factors correctly.
For a rectangular prism with length factor a and width factor b but fixed height, volume factor is ab. For a cylinder, scaling radius by a and height by b produces factor a²b.
Compare independently constructed boxes and cylinders before and after scaling. A teacher reviews which dimension labels were changed and why factors multiply.

Original first-party Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, 2017–2019 (CC BY 4.0), source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/18/preparation.html . No publisher figures or branded assessment tasks are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Prism scale product
KeyConcepts.Definition: Scale two independent linear dimensions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cylinder scale product
KeyConcepts.Definition: Radius factor a and height factor b.

KeyConcepts.Title: Uniform 3D scaling
KeyConcepts.Definition: All linear dimensions scaled by same k.
KeyConcepts.Example: A similar solid doubled in all dimensions has eightfold volume.

WorkedExamples.Title: Two box dimensions
WorkedExamples.Question: Box 2×3×4: double length and triple width, same height. New V?

WorkedExamples.Title: Radius and height
WorkedExamples.Question: Cylinder original volume 5π; double radius and triple height. New volume?
Steps: Total volume factor 12, so new V=60π.

WorkedExamples.Title: All dimensions doubled
WorkedExamples.Question: Solid volume 7 cm³ undergoes uniform scale factor 2. New volume?
Steps: Each of three independent dimensions doubles.
WorkedExamples.Check: A scale factor of 2 is not a volume factor of 2.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Adding instead of multiplying scale factors.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Independent dimensions multiply in volume.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forgetting radius square in cylinder scaling.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Circular base area depends on r².

SummaryPoints: A cylinder radius factor is squared.
Uniform 3D scale k changes volume by k³.

Lessons.Title: Estimating a Hemisphere
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: estimate the volume of a hemisphere using comparisons with familiar cylindrical and conical volumes and explain the limitations of estimates.
A hemisphere is half a sphere. A careful comparison can bound its volume using a surrounding cylinder, but numerical experiments alone do not constitute a proof of the exact sphere formula.

Draw a hemisphere of radius 3 fitting inside a cylinder with radius 3 and height 3. Estimate an upper bound of 27π cm³, then discuss that the exact hemisphere volume is 18π cm³. A teacher checks the conceptual diagram and assumptions.

Original first-party Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, 2017–2019 (CC BY 4.0), source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/19/preparation.html . No publisher figures or branded assessment tasks are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Hemisphere
KeyConcepts.Definition: Half of a sphere cut through its center.

KeyConcepts.Title: Containing cylinder
KeyConcepts.Definition: A hemisphere radius r fits inside a cylinder radius r, height r.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Cylinder volume πr³ is an upper bound.

KeyConcepts.Title: Exact hemisphere formula
KeyConcepts.Definition: Half of 4πr³/3.

WorkedExamples.Title: Cylinder bound
WorkedExamples.Question: Radius 3 hemisphere inside same-radius height-3 cylinder. What cylinder volume?
WorkedExamples.Check: The hemisphere fits inside the cylinder.

WorkedExamples.Title: Exact hemisphere volume
WorkedExamples.Question: Find hemisphere volume when r=3.
WorkedExamples.Check: It is below the 27π cylinder bound.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare volumes
WorkedExamples.Question: What fraction of the containing radius-r height-r cylinder does the hemisphere occupy?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating the bounding cylinder volume as exact hemisphere volume.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A hemisphere leaves unfilled corner regions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use bound only as a comparison.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling an experimental fill ratio a rigorous proof.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Empirical measurements have error.

SummaryPoints: A hemisphere is half a sphere.

Lessons.Title: The Volume of a Sphere
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: develop and apply the relationship between sphere radius and volume, including the cubic effect of scaling radius.
Sphere volume is V=4πr³/3. Distinguish radius from diameter and compare with the hemisphere volume. Doubling radius multiplies sphere volume by eight, not two.
Use a first-party diagram of a sphere and its central great circle. Label r and calculate volume at r=3; teacher review checks spatial reasoning and measurement annotation.

Original first-party Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, 2017–2019 (CC BY 4.0), source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/20/preparation.html . No publisher figures or branded assessment tasks are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sphere volume
KeyConcepts.Definition: The volume inside a sphere of radius r.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cubic radius scaling
KeyConcepts.Definition: Radius enters as r³.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Scale r by k, V changes by k³.

KeyConcepts.Title: Diameter relation
KeyConcepts.Definition: The diameter is twice radius.

WorkedExamples.Title: Volume at radius 3
WorkedExamples.Question: Sphere radius 3 cm. Find exact volume.

WorkedExamples.Title: Radius from diameter
WorkedExamples.Question: Sphere diameter 10 cm. Find its exact volume.
WorkedExamples.Check: Using diameter directly would be eight times too large.

WorkedExamples.Title: Double radius
WorkedExamples.Question: Sphere volume 12π at radius r. Radius doubles. New volume?
WorkedExamples.Check: Sphere volume is cubic in radius.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Squaring radius instead of cubing it.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Sphere volume has three dimensions.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Substituting diameter for radius.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Diameter is double and changes volume eightfold.

SummaryPoints: Use cubic units and correct radius.

Visuals.Title: Sphere volume proportional to radius cubed
Visuals.Description: V=(4/3)πr³. The table shows exact volume coefficients, not decimals.

Lessons.Title: Cylinders, Cones, and Spheres
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: select and compare the appropriate volume formulas for cylinders, cones and spheres, including composite or missing-capacity situations.
For a cylinder and cone with the same r,h, the cone has one third the cylinder volume. A sphere of radius r requires a cubic radius term and does not depend on an independent cylinder height.
Create a labeled table with one solid of each type, compute volumes and justify the formula selected. Teacher review checks diagrams, units and how the chosen measurements correspond to each solid.

Original first-party Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, 2017–2019 (CC BY 4.0), source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/21/preparation.html . No publisher figures or branded assessment tasks are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cylinder formula
KeyConcepts.Definition: Prism-like circular stack.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cone formula
KeyConcepts.Definition: One-third same-r and same-h cylinder.

KeyConcepts.Title: Sphere formula
KeyConcepts.Definition: Round 3D solid depending on radius.

WorkedExamples.Title: Cylinder calculation
WorkedExamples.Question: Cylinder r=2,h=6. What volume?

WorkedExamples.Title: Cone calculation
WorkedExamples.Question: Cone r=2,h=6. What volume?
WorkedExamples.Check: Cone is one-third the same-base cylinder.

WorkedExamples.Title: Sphere calculation
WorkedExamples.Question: Sphere radius 3. What volume?

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using cylinder formula on a cone.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Cone volume is one third.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Identify the solid type before selecting a formula.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Equating sphere radius to an unrelated cylinder height.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Sphere has no independent axial height in formula.

SummaryPoints: Choose volume formula from solid geometry.

Lessons.Title: Volume As a Function of . . .
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: compare volume as a function of water height or shape dimensions, explaining which relationships are linear and which are nonlinear.

For a cylinder with fixed radius, water volume V(h)=πr²h grows linearly with height. For a cone filled from the narrow tip upward, the water surface radius increases proportionally with water height; the filled volume grows as h³ when the container shape is fixed.

Sketch volume-height graphs for a cylinder and an upright cone with the same total height. Explain why equal height increments need different volume increments in the cone. Teacher review is essential for diagram orientation, modeling assumptions and graph shape.

Original first-party Edulytiks instruction informed by Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics Grade 8, 2017–2019 (CC BY 4.0), source https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/22/preparation.html . No publisher figures or branded assessment tasks are reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cylinder volume versus height
KeyConcepts.Definition: Fixed cross-sectional area produces a linear function.

KeyConcepts.Title: Cone from tip versus height
KeyConcepts.Definition: Similar cross-sections grow with water height.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Filled volume proportional to h³ for fixed cone proportions.
KeyConcepts.Example: Doubling water height from tip multiplies filled volume by 8, while still below brim.

KeyConcepts.Title: Interpreting graph slope
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rate of volume added per height increase equals cross-sectional area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For widening shape, slope increases with height.
KeyConcepts.Example: Near cone tip, tiny area gives slow volume increase.

WorkedExamples.Title: Cylinder volume function
WorkedExamples.Question: Cylinder radius 2 cm. Express V at water height h and find V(3).
WorkedExamples.Check: Volume-height graph is a line through origin.

WorkedExamples.Title: Cone fill scaling
WorkedExamples.Question: In a conical vessel filled from tip, similar filled volumes at heights h and 2h have what ratio?
Steps: Radius scales with height for similar cross-sections.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find volume at higher height
WorkedExamples.Question: Cone filled from tip has volume 3 cm³ at height 2 cm. Predict volume at height 4 cm within the same cone.
WorkedExamples.Method: Apply cubic scaling for similar filled cones.
WorkedExamples.Check: Valid only for a cone with tip at bottom and height 4 within its walls.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming any container produces a linear volume-height relation.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Changing cross-section makes slope variable.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using h³ for a cylinder of fixed radius.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Its area does not vary with water height.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use linear V=Ah for fixed area.

SummaryPoints: Volume-height functions depend on container geometry.
Fixed-area cylinders are linear in h.
Tip-up conical fill volumes scale cubically.

Visuals.Title: Cylinder water volume as height rises
Visuals.Description: With fixed radius 2, water volume V=4πh.
